paragraphs: One-sentence judgement: an astronomer does not simply look at stars but observes, researches and interprets astronomical phenomena, turns observational or simulated data into reviewable conclusions, and keeps the data, code, papers and conclusions consistent with one another. The role links observation and data acquisition, modelling and validation, instrument and software development, and review and communication into a traceable chain of evidence; people who only want to look at pretty pictures and are unwilling to accept peer review and data checking are not suited.

Signals for continued exploration: you are willing to break a research question into testable hypotheses, keep written records of data sources, processing steps and uncertainty, use code or statistical methods to check your own conclusions, and accept review comments and public challenge and revise accordingly; you are also willing to stay patient during long explorations with no direct return.

Conditions for pausing investment first: you have not yet completed a full-process exercise from question through data and analysis and review to writing, or you can only rely on others to judge whether the data and conclusions are reliable; also do not treat astrophotography as a hobby, an interest in science videos or a short online course certificate as proof of research ability.

Education and training must be checked separately: O*NET lists 19-2011.00 as Job Zone Five (SVP 8.0 and above), and among respondents 65% consider a doctorate necessary, 26% consider postdoctoral training necessary and 9% consider a master's necessary; but a qualification does not equal a post appointment, funding or data authority. Observing time, dataset access and telescope operating authority are allocated by institutions, and this page provides no hiring, competition or authorisation standard.

In one sentence: this is a research post centred on observation and data processing, theoretical or simulation validation, and writing results into reviewable outputs and peer communication. Competence depends on methodological rigour, reviewable data and code and honest reporting of uncertainty, not personality labels or a love of the stars.

The work of astronomers falls into four categories: observation and data acquisition (using ground-based and space telescopes and various scientific instruments to study celestial phenomena and measure radio, infrared, gamma and X-ray radiation); analysis and modelling (using computers to analyse research data, compute orbits and determine the size, shape, brightness and motion of celestial bodies, and to build and test theories); instruments and software (developing the instruments and software needed for astronomical observation and analysis); and review, teaching and communication (publishing papers and conference reports, supervising students, teaching, reviewing proposals and papers, securing funding, and taking part in professional committees and public outreach). All four categories require reviewable methods and traceable data and must be carried out within research ethics and data authority.

O*NET19-2011.00 (updated 2026) is defined as observing, researching and interpreting astronomical phenomena to increase basic knowledge or solve practical problems, and lists 17 tasks. details provides Importance ratings, for example computer analysis of data 93, publishing research 91 and telescope research 88, which are not frequency of occurrence or a hiring threshold.

Confirm the data source, usage licence and publication deadline; protected observations, proprietary periods up to publication and restricted datasets must be handled according to institutional and project rules, and authority must not be bypassed or content published early.

Data, code and conclusions must be presented truthfully, and authorship and contributions determined according to the norms; data must not be reported selectively, nor conclusions written by another person or changed afterwards without a trace.
Pay and working hours

Posts with the same title may use an annual salary, project funding or a fixed-term contract; when comparing, include the contract term, funding source, observing and teaching duties, and night shift and travel arrangements in the written conditions, not only the nominal annual salary.

Takes computational methods and information systems as the research object and outputs algorithms, systems and software; astronomers take celestial phenomena as the research object, and computational methods are only a means of reaching scientific conclusions.

If you would rather develop computational methods and information systems themselves, compare computer and information research scientists first; if you would rather use computational means to answer questions about celestial phenomena, astronomy suits you.
Researching and developing computational methods, algorithms and information systems, with outputs mainly methods papers, systems and software.
Astronomers and computer and information research scientists

Takes mathematical structures, theorems and proofs as the core output, where the proof itself is the conclusion; astronomers explain celestial phenomena with observational evidence, and the conclusion must be consistent with the data.
If you would rather work on abstract structures and rigorous proofs, compare mathematicians first; if you would rather have conclusions tested against observational data, astronomy suits you.
Researching mathematical structures and proving theorems, with outputs mainly theorems, proofs and methods papers.
Astronomers and mathematicians

Focuses on statistical inference and method application and provides analysis and experimental design support to others; astronomers themselves carry the complete chain from observation to conclusion.
If you would rather do statistical methods and data analysis support, compare statisticians first; if you would rather complete the research loop independently, astronomy suits you.
Designing sampling and analysis methods, modelling and interpreting data, with outputs mainly statistical analysis and method application.
Astronomers and statisticians
Focuses on data modelling and business or product problems, where the evaluation criteria often include practical effect; astronomers focus on scientific questions and evidence standards.
If you would rather use data to solve business or product problems, compare data scientists first; if you would rather use data to answer scientific questions, astronomy suits you.
Building and evaluating data models and constructing data pipelines, with outputs mainly models, metrics and data products.
Astronomers and data scientists

The research objects are broader, covering physical systems from particles to condensed matter and often involving experimental apparatus; astronomers focus on celestial bodies and phenomena at cosmic scales.
If you would rather study a broader range of physical systems and experiments, compare physicists first; if you would rather take celestial bodies as the research object, astronomy suits you.
Designing and running physics experiments or theoretical models, with outputs mainly physics conclusions and experimental methods.
Astronomers and physicists
Focuses on observing and forecasting the Earth and space environment, with users including operational and public decision making; astronomers focus on basic scientific questions.
If you would rather do environmental observation and forecasting, compare atmospheric and space scientists first; if you would rather do basic scientific exploration, astronomy suits you.
Observing and simulating the Earth and space environment and issuing forecasts, with outputs mainly observational data, models and forecasts.
Astronomers and atmospheric and space scientists

entries.answer: Astronomers observe, research and interpret astronomical phenomena: studying celestial bodies with ground-based and space telescopes and scientific instruments, measuring radio and infrared and other radiation, using computers to analyse research data, computing orbits and celestial parameters, building and testing theories, and writing the results into papers and conference reports, reviewing proposals and papers, supervising students and carrying out public outreach. It is not simply looking at stars but making the data, methods and conclusions into a reviewable chain of evidence.
entries.question: What does an astronomer do every day?

entries.answer: Computer and information research scientists take computational methods and information systems as their object; mathematicians take mathematical structures and proofs; statisticians focus on statistical inference and method application; data scientists focus on data modelling and business problems; physicists study a broader range of physical systems and experiments; atmospheric and space scientists focus on observing and forecasting the Earth and space environment. Astronomers take the observation, research and interpretation of celestial phenomena as their core; adjacent occupations also use data and computation, but the evidence standards and responsibility boundaries of their research objects differ.

entries.answer: Six types of risk need to be judged in advance: data processing and code errors, observation and instrument abnormalities, research integrity and authorship problems, leakage of protected or proprietary data, misstatement in public communication and teaching, and station site and night shift safety. The control method is to verify by method, keep reproducible records, report by procedure and accept peer review.

entries.answer: The data shown by O*NET give about 1,800 employed in 19-2011.00 for this occupation in 2024, projected growth of 1%—2% for 2024—2034 and about 100 job openings over the projection period; the BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook gives, on the combined physicists and astronomers measure, 7% growth for 2025—2035 and about 1,500 openings per year on average. Directions one can transfer to include computer and information research scientists, mathematicians, statisticians, data scientists, physicists, atmospheric and space scientists, geoscientists and postsecondary physics teachers, but the method requirements and responsibility boundaries of each direction differ.

entries.answer: Common misconceptions include: that liking the night sky or enjoying astrophotography as a hobby is enough to enter a research post (in fact systematic research training and method ability are needed); that the occupation is mainly night visual observation (in fact a large amount of time goes into data processing, programming and analysis); that a degree automatically brings observing time, funding or authorship eligibility (in fact these are allocated by institutions and projects); and that AI has already wholly replaced this occupation (in fact the official projection is 1%—2% growth for this occupation in 2024—2034 and 7% growth for the combined occupation group in 2025—2035, and task automation does not equal the disappearance of jobs).

subject.summary: Astronomers observe, research and interpret astronomical phenomena, turn observational or simulated data into reviewable conclusions, and keep the data, code, papers and conclusions consistent with one another. On the US side this corresponds to O*NET 19-2011.00 (Astronomers), usually entered with doctoral-level training; O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Five (SVP 8.0 and above). Mainland China statistics aggregate by industry sector and do not list this occupation separately, so industry figures serve only as a comparison.
